history.heading: The Piast kingdom
paragraphs: Slavic tribes settled the lands of present-day Poland in the early Middle Ages. In 966 Duke Mieszko I of the Piast dynasty was baptised, marking the founding of the Polish state, and in 1025 Bolesław I was crowned the first king. Kraków became the royal capital, and its old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Under Casimir III the Great in the 14th century, Poland flourished and welcomed Jewish communities, which grew into the largest in Europe.

history.heading: The Commonwealth
paragraphs: The union with Lithuania, begun in 1386 under the Jagiellonian dynasty, became the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, one of Europe's largest and most diverse states. Its nobility elected kings and enjoyed broad freedoms. Nicolaus Copernicus proposed his heliocentric theory there. King Jan III Sobieski helped defeat the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683.

The Commonwealth adopted Europe's first modern written constitution on 3 May 1791, but it was weakened by internal divisions and partitioned three times by Russia, Prussia and Austria, disappearing from the map in 1795.

history.heading: Rebirth, war and communism
paragraphs: After over a century of partition and failed uprisings, Poland regained independence on 11 November 1918 and defeated the Red Army in 1920. In September 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union invaded, starting the Second World War. Germany built extermination camps on Polish soil, including Auschwitz, where most of Poland's three million Jews and millions of others were murdered. About one-sixth of Poland's population died, and Warsaw was destroyed after the 1944 uprising.

After the war Poland's borders were shifted westward, and a Soviet-backed communist regime took power. The election of Polish Pope John Paul II in 1978 and the Solidarity trade union movement, led by Lech Wałęsa from 1980, challenged communist rule.

history.heading: Democratic Poland
paragraphs: In 1989 round-table talks led to partly free elections and the first non-communist government in the Soviet bloc. Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004 and became one of Europe's fastest-growing economies. Since 2022 it has hosted millions of Ukrainian refugees and become a key supporter of Ukraine.

culture.heading: Faith and culture
paragraphs: Polish is a West Slavic language. Poland is one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, and the Church has played an important role in national identity. Famous Poles include Frédéric Chopin, Marie Curie (the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences), and writers Henryk Sienkiewicz, Wisława Szymborska and Olga Tokarczuk, all Nobel laureates.
Polish cinema, with directors such as Andrzej Wajda and Krzysztof Kieślowski, is highly regarded, and the video game The Witcher was made in Poland.

culture.heading: Food and traditions
paragraphs: Polish cuisine includes pierogi (dumplings), bigos (hunter's stew), żurek (sour rye soup), kiełbasa sausage and pączki doughnuts. Christmas Eve (Wigilia) with twelve dishes is the most important family celebration. Football, volleyball and ski jumping are popular.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Poland is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Sejm (lower house), while the directly elected president can veto laws. Politics has been sharply polarised between the conservative Law and Justice party (PiS), which governed from 2015 to 2023 and was criticised by the EU over judicial reforms, and the liberal Civic Coalition led by Donald Tusk, which returned to power in 2023.
Conservative Karol Nawrocki won the 2025 presidential election. Poland spends a larger share of its economy on defence than any other NATO member.

economy.heading: A post-communist success
paragraphs: Poland has one of the largest economies in the EU and is often cited as the most successful post-communist economy; it avoided recession during the 2008 financial crisis. Key sectors include manufacturing (cars, appliances, furniture and batteries), food processing, IT and business services, logistics and agriculture.
Poland uses the złoty rather than the euro. It is moving away from coal, which long dominated its energy supply, toward renewables and nuclear power.
